A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study despite the title and model renaming. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-modeling evaluations, speculative-decoding measurements and fMRI prediction analyses in Tables 1–3 and the appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains original language-modeling and fMRI results and adds training ablations, component comparisons and decoding measurements.

M1.justification: Induction-only becomes GIM, while the combined Induction-Gram corresponds to Infini-gram with GIM. The matching procedures, fuzzy-model architecture and losses, switching rule in Equation (5), and fMRI feature construction remain unchanged. The new training variants are ablations rather than revisions to the proposed method.

E1.justification: v2 adds training the fuzzy matcher on the legal-domain Pile-of-Law corpus in Appendix A.2. The existing language datasets and the fMRI evaluation on subject UTS03 remain. Suggested applications to other sequential domains are not evaluated.

E2.justification: v2 Section 4.1 adds a standard 5-gram comparison, reporting 26.4% on Pile-val versus Infini-gram's 27.1%. Table A4 also adds TinyLLaMA-1.1B to the H100 comparisons with LLaMA2-13B and LLaMA2-70B; v1 Table 2 included TinyLLaMA only in the A40 comparisons.

E3.justification: New BabyLM evaluations introduce controlled variations in positional encoding, distillation losses and component inclusion. Speculative decoding additionally reports acceptance rate. The retained stated context lengths, splits, generation budgets and hardware settings are unchanged; the additions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's exact/fuzzy comparisons and threshold analysis, v2 Tables A1–A3 systematically test positional encoding, loss combinations, training-corpus sensitivity and removal of individual prediction components. These substantially expand validation of the design choices. The examples in v2 Figure 5 were already present in v1 Figure A2.

E5.justification: Both versions report three decoding runs with different seeds and means with standard deviations, fMRI results with 95% confidence intervals, and the same binomial test. New decoding entries follow the existing reporting practice; no new uncertainty-estimation procedure or increased run count is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial ablation results: Table A1 reports 43.2% versus 37.0% for relative versus sinusoidal encoding, and Table A2 reports 43.2%, 42.7% and 41.8% for OpenWebText, Pile-train and Pile-of-Law training. Component-removal results, acceptance rates and additional comparator timings are also new. These are additional conditions, not improvements over v1's matched models; the main language and fMRI table values remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The similarity definitions, weighted counts, prediction distributions and switching rule in Equations (1)–(5) are retained, as is the fMRI encoding formulation. Neither version adds theoretical results, proofs or new formal assumptions.

C1.justification: The headline contribution shifts from the combined Induction-Gram language model to GIM as a standalone module, with Infini-gram presented as one integration. Speculative-decoding acceleration leaves the abstract, and v2 explicitly disclaims parity with black-box LLMs. The central interpretability and language/fMRI improvement claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning loss complementarity, domain-specific training, compensation between matching components, and fast decoding despite lower acceptance rates. Section 5.2 more explicitly links cortical prediction improvements to contextual language processing. The existing short-context and reasoning limitations remain, with additional prospective applications discussed.

D1.justification: v2 documents the new ablation configurations and changes the advertised code repository from induction-gram to generalized-induction-head. However, it omits v1's decoding sample counts: six BabyLM prompts and 100 prompts each for FineWeb and Pile. Core architecture, optimizer, training-budget and hardware disclosures remain.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around inherently interpretable modules and evaluation through neuroscience applications. It adds interpretability-evaluation literature, including Adebayo et al. and Doshi-Velez and Kim, further mechanistic and neuroscience work, and connections to other sequential domains. Conversely, v1's REST and foundational speculative-decoding references are removed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and substantial portions of the related work and discussion are rewritten around GIM. Infini-gram integration moves into the language experiments, speculative decoding moves to Appendix A.5, and existing qualitative examples enter the main text. An impact statement and conference checklist are added.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the pipeline around the standalone GIM module, adds an fMRI feature-construction diagram and three ablation tables, and expands the decoding table with acceptance columns and comparator rows. Existing examples are redistributed and annotated, while the fMRI table and cortical visualization are arranged side by side.

improvement.justification: Tables A1–A3 better support the training and component choices, while acceptance rates and additional TinyLLaMA comparisons make efficiency results more informative. The revised exposition and fMRI diagram improve clarity. These are useful incremental gains over the retained main findings, partly offset by the omission of decoding prompt counts.
